title: The Value Illusion
text:
Preface
These are field notes from poking R until the abstractions confessed, and then asking what that confession is for.
The session that started them had no plan. It called .Internal(inspect()) on NULL, on list(), on a hand-built S3 object, on an environment, on bit64::integer64(), on an S7 class, on an R6 generator, on a weak reference. It pasted the dumps back into the file and argued with them in the comments. The argument turned out to be an old one, wearing new syntax: value against identity, signal against unwind, representation against type, and the question of where a name is allowed to mean only one kind of thing.
That sentence organizes the metal. The sentence that organizes the work you do with the metal is shorter, and it showed up later in the same conversation, once the dumps had stopped being the point:
Object-oriented or functional is a choice of machinery under that law. The data you have to represent drives the names. Functions compose the workflows the data flows through. Everything else in this book is a consequence, a source, or a place the consequence gets sharp.

title: The Value Illusion
section: What kind of claim this is
text:
What kind of claim this is
Four registers, and they are not interchangeable.
A mechanism is something a manual or the R sources state. The claim that there is exactly one NILSXP, R_NilValue, is a mechanism. It lives in R Internals for R 4.6.1, and the initialization in memory.c is blunt about it: that node has to be the first cons cell allocated, or armageddon happens.
A probe is something a session actually printed. identical(NULL, c()) is TRUE. identical(NULL, list()) is FALSE. An S7 instance changed address across @p <-. Those are facts about a session, and the small verification script re-checks the ones that do not depend on a particular IDE.
A reading is an interpretation that the mechanism and the probe support. “Empty list() is a zero of the generic-vector type, and that fact is older and deeper than S3 dispatch” is a reading. It can be argued with.
A recommendation is a way to build. “A client is a handle; a config is a value” is a recommendation. It is earned by the reading, and it can be overruled for a stated reason.
The chapters mix the four on purpose. When a sentence is doing one of them, it should be possible to tell. The inquiry ledger is where a reading is still soft.

title: The Value Illusion
text:
What this is next to
The design manual for the type-driven half of this taste already exists, and this book does not pretend to replace it: S7 Design Notes. That book asks what knowledge a model can carry so the rest of the program stops rediscovering it. This one asks what the runtime is already carrying, and which design habits are a truce with that runtime rather than a fight with it.
Advanced R remains the best long-form map of names and values, environments, object systems, and conditions. R Internals is the document these notes keep going back to, with the warning printed in the manual itself: it is a work in progress and should be checked against the source. Where the two disagree with a dump, the dump wins for that session and the source wins for the mechanism.

title: The Value Illusion
text:
How to read
Read The Law if you read one chapter. It is the whole argument in miniature.
The metal chapters are a guided decoding of inspect output: the header, the three different empties, cons cells against generic vectors, the machinery under copy-on-modify, the SEXP types you only meet in the right context, and the condition system people keep using as if it were Java.
The hybrid chapters are historical, with the romance scraped off. R was built for a conversation with data. That is why the REPL is so good, and why a production package has to impose contracts the language will not impose for you.
The taste chapters are the part that should change how a package is shaped: open verbs, where state is allowed to live, runtime types as a substitute for a missing schema layer, presentation as part of the contract, and the data-driven close.
The lab notebook walks the original probes in order, including the hypothesis that did not survive the next call. That failure is the best thing in the file.
Private chat is not evidence here. The probes, the manuals, and the papers are. Where a conclusion is the author’s taste, it is labeled as taste.

title: 1  The Law
text:
1.1 Name it
The dumps and the design argument are the same conversation seen at two distances.
Up close, R is a heap of tagged nodes, a generational collector, a reference count, a promise, and a handful of objects that really are mutable. From a package away, the useful question is which of your names are allowed to be those mutable objects, and which names are facts that must survive being passed around, printed, tested, and serialized.
Hold both distances at once and a law falls out. It is not an R law. It is a law about programs that have to stay honest while the data is still being discovered.
A name is a decision that a concept exists.
api_config is a decision. color is a decision. status_code is a decision if a bare integer would lie. The ubiquitous language Eric Evans described in Domain-Driven Design for large domains is the same discipline scaled down to one package, or one person’s system: the words in the code, the words in the console, and the words in your head are the same words, and you curate them. You do not inherit a vocabulary by subclassing someone else’s nouns. You write one, and you keep it small enough to defend.
Naming is also the encapsulation. A prefix, a package namespace, and a stable verb are how a reader finds the operation. api_config_new, req_headers, format.foo — the module is the vocabulary, not a living object you have to open to discover what it can do. Shells have worked this way for decades. So do the R APIs that people actually love to call.

title: 1  The Law
text:
1.2 Admit only valid values
A name that accepts anything is a comment.
The standard worth stealing is Alexis King’s, from Parse, don’t validate: construction is the check. Downstream code receives a value that already means the name, and it stops re-asking. In a language with a real type checker this is a theorem. In R it is a ritual you can house in an S3 constructor (new_*, validate_*, as_*) or in an S7 property and a class validator. The housing is a tradeoff, discussed in Chapter 12. The requirement is not. If the work is production work, invalid states are a bug at the boundary, not a vibe you check in the third method that happens to care.
R will not make you do this. That is the whole difficulty, and it is also why the REPL is such a good place to discover which names deserve the ceremony. Discovery first. Then the parse.

title: 1  The Law
text:
1.3 Show it well
A type is not done when it can be constructed. It is done when a human can see what it means.
R already treats the console as a user interface: print, format, str, and the semantic vocabulary in cli. PowerShell went further and made the view a separate, declarative contract (format data, sitting on the Monad manifesto’s rule that the pipe carries objects and the host decides how they look). The idea travels even though the XML does not. Skipping format is the same kind of unfinished as skipping the validator: the value exists, and nobody can read it.
Effects need the same courtesy. A warning, a progress meter, a verbose trace, and a fatal error are different channels. Smashing them into cat() throws away the only protocol R has for routing them. That protocol is the condition system, and it is closer to Common Lisp than the tryCatch habit suggests. Chapter 7 goes into it.

title: 1  The Law
text:
1.4 Extend it with verbs
The operation is the extension point.
R’s generic-function tradition (S3, S4, S7) and the trait tradition in Rust share a posture: a new package can teach an old verb a new noun, or teach an old noun a new verb, without owning the type’s method table. Message-passing objects invert the posture. The type owns the verbs, and extension leans on subclassing or patching. Both are legitimate. They fit different problems. Data work, HTTP, compilers, and tool-using models are usually algebras — verbs closed over types — and they want the open verb. Widgets, documents with identity, and long-lived sessions sometimes want the closed object. R lets you build either, which is freedom and also how a codebase loses the plot.
The practical shape that keeps showing up:





flowchart LR
  data[Domain data] --> names[Names]
  names --> types[Values that admit only those names]
  types --> verbs[Verbs and generics]
  types --> views[Print, format, cli]
  verbs --> workflows[Workflows as composition]
  handles[Handles at the edge] --> workflows
  views --> host[The host]






Values in the middle. Handles at the rim, where identity is load-bearing: a socket, a token that refreshes, a cache, a conversation. Verbs everywhere a human or a pipe might call them. Views at the host.

title: 1  The Law
text:
1.5 Two sentences, one book
Chambers compressed S and R into three principles, restated in S, R, and Data Science: everything that exists is an object, everything that happens is a function call, and interfaces to other languages are part of the language. The law above is what those principles feel like when you are the one shipping the package.
The metal chapters show why the value illusion holds, and where it is contractually false. The hybrid chapters show why the language grew this shape and why rigor feels like swimming upstream. The taste chapters are the law applied: containers, runtime types, presentation, dispatch.
If you remember one recommendation, remember the split. Facts are values. Capabilities are handles. Functions are the user interface. The console is a view, not a leftover.

title: 2  The Header
text:
2.1 The type tag is five bits
inspect is not a closure you can open in the editor. It is a C entry, do_inspect, living in src/main/inspect.c and reached through .Internal. The thing being printed is a node on the heap. The line you get back is the node’s header, translated into a dialect that rewards a little memorization.
A typical line from a length-one integer inside a classed list:
Read it left to right.
The manual’s version of this layout is R Internals, section 1.1. The header changed shape in R 3.5.0. Older blog posts that describe a 32-bit sxpinfo are describing a previous machine.
SEXPTYPE occupies the first five bits, so there is room for 32 tags. The table in the manual is the one to trust. The ones a session like this actually meets:
Codes 11 and 12 are a genuine piece of archaeology, not a rumor. The manual says they were used for internal factors and ordered factors, and were withdrawn. The numbers survive in serialized objects, so the gap cannot be casually reused. Factors today are integers with attributes. That story is in Chapter 6. OBJSXP used to be spelled S4SXP; the comment is still sitting in sexptype2char.
There is also a pseudo-type FUNSXP with code 99, used in a few internal tables to mean “some kind of function.” You will not see it in an inspect line. ANYSXP (18) is a placeholder for “any argument,” and there are no objects of that type.

title: 2  The Header
text:
2.2 g0c1 is two different fields
The generation and the class are neighbors in the printout and unrelated in the header.
gcgen is one bit. Inspect prints it as g0 or g1. It will never print g2. The collector behind that bit is a young space plus two old generations (NUM_OLD_GENERATIONS is 2), and gc() walks three collection levels. A node in the young space and a node in old generation 0 can both print g0, so the digit is not a synonym for “just allocated.” Long-lived startup nodes — R_NilValue, locked symbols, cached CHARSXPs — print g1 in practice. That is a tendency in the dumps, not a definition of the bit. Treat a blog post that decodes g0c1 as “generation 0 of 3, size class 1 of a vague scale” as out of date.
gccls is three bits, so eight allocation classes. The manual’s allocation-class section and the comment in memory.c agree:







Class
What lives there




0
Non-vector nodes, and the zero-size bucket


1–5
Small vectors, with room for 8, 16, 32, 64, and 128 bytes


6
Custom allocators (allocVector3), not counted as ordinary R memory


7
Large vectors, malloc’d individually



That is the whole of “random access versus cons” as a memory-manager question, and it is not stack versus heap. A pairlist node is class 0 because it is not a vector. A length-one integer is class 1 because four payload bytes fit in the 8-byte bucket. A length-one character vector is also class 1: one pointer. An environment’s hash table of a few dozen slots is class 7: twenty-nine pointers do not fit in 128 bytes. Empty character() and empty integer() landed in class 0 in the dumps, because a zero-length vector has nothing to put in a data page.
Small vectors come out of pages of about 2000 bytes. Large ones are their own allocations. Custom-allocator vectors can share memory in ways R’s accounting refuses to pretend to understand. ALTREP, later, is a further escape hatch: the node can exist before the data does.

title: 2  The Header
section: 2.3 The flags are the header talking
text:
2.3 The flags are the header talking
The bracket is a selection, not a full register dump. The fields live in the 64-bit sxpinfo structure quoted in the manual:
SEXPTYPE type      :  5;
unsigned int scalar:  1;
unsigned int obj   :  1;  /* class attribute? */
unsigned int alt   :  1;  /* ALTREP? */
unsigned int gp    : 16;
unsigned int mark  :  1;
unsigned int debug :  1;
unsigned int trace :  1;
unsigned int spare :  1;
unsigned int gcgen :  1;
unsigned int gccls :  3;
unsigned int named : 16;  /* the reference count, these days */
The flags worth knowing by sight:







Flag
Meaning




OBJ
The obj bit. This is what is.object() answers. A class attribute sets it.


ATT
The attribute pointer is not Nil. Attributes are a pairlist.


MARK
The collector has marked the node in this collection.


REF(n)
The reference count.


LCK
Locked. Common on symbols and on locked bindings or environments.


gp=0x…
Sixteen general-purpose bits. Their meaning depends on the type.


ALT
Not always spelled that way in the bracket, but the alt bit is how ALTREP is recognized.


GL
Shows up on the global environment in inspect output.



gp is where people get inventive, and it is worth resisting. On a CHARSXP the inspect line often already translates the bits you care about: [ASCII] [cached], sometimes with ATT because the character cache hangs information off the attribute pointer. The manual has a section on CHARSXP encodings and another on the cache. Symbol gp values (0x4000, 0x6000, 0x7000, 0x8000 in the dumps) are a different code book. They are decoded in the source, not in a stable user manual, and this book leaves them on the open list rather than inventing a table.

title: 2  The Header
text:
2.4 REF(65535) is a saturated count
NAMED_BITS is 16. Under the reference-counting build, REFCNTMAX is (1 << 16) - 1, which is 65535. MARK_NOT_MUTABLE sets the count to that ceiling. Incrementing past the ceiling is a no-op, and decrementing a saturated count is also a no-op: the macros in Defn.h refuse to move a count that has hit the cap. A saturated node stays saturated. That is the technical meaning of immortal in these notes. The collector is not invited to free it, and the copy-on-modify logic is not invited to mutate it.
R_NilValue is constructed that way on purpose. So are a lot of other process-lifetime nodes: many symbols, R_TrueValue, R_FalseValue, the canonical logical NA. A high count on a value you just created is a different phenomenon. It means something in the process is holding the node. The evaluator, the protection stack, .Last.value, a promise, an attribute, an environment binding, and an IDE’s object browser all count. The same binding can print REF(1) in a quiet console and a much larger number under RStudio, because RStudio is a holder. The count is a census of current pointers. It is not a property of the source literal.
do_inspect prints REF(n) only when the count is nonzero. The test in src/main/inspect.c is if (REFCNT(v)). A fresh unshared vector with no other flags therefore shows an empty bracket, [], which is what the empty vectors in the session did. The field is still there, and it is zero. On a normal build you will not see the old NAM(n) token at all. That spelling belongs to the legacy NAMED compile, not to the reference-counting one you are running.

title: 2  The Header
text:
2.5 Where inspect sits
The symbol inspect in the internal table is a SYMSXP whose internal pointer aims at that C routine. You do not hold the printer as a value in the way you hold the vector you asked it to describe. .Internal and .Primitive are the subject of chapter 2 of the same manual. Primitives are the fast path. Internals are the slightly more ordinary one. Neither is “an R function that happens to be written in C” in the way a .Call wrapper is. They are entries in the interpreter’s own table.
One more ambiguity the manual states cleanly, because the dumps make it easy to miss: an environment is both a frame and an enclosure. The frame is the bindings. The enclosure is the parent you walk when a name is missing. Hash tables, when present, are a VECSXP of pairlists, and the empty buckets are the Nil singleton, over and over, at one address. That picture is the whole of the next two chapters.

title: 3  Three Empties
text:
3.1 Why Nil gets to be the only one
The first good hypothesis in the notebook was slightly too wide, and the next calls retired the extra width. That is the experiment working.
The hypothesis, paraphrased from the comments: any genuinely empty thing is the same immortal NILSXP cell. NULL, c(), and pairlist() confirmed it, including under the strictest identical() switches. extptr.as.ref = TRUE does not add anything to that comparison: neither value is an external pointer, so the flag never gets a chance to matter. Same address. Same type code 0. REF pinned at the ceiling. is.pairlist(NULL) is true, because Nil is the empty pairlist. is.list(NULL) is false, because a list is a generic vector and Nil is not one.
Then list() and alist() printed a different address, type 19, VECSXP, length 0, empty flag bracket. Then integer(), character(), double(), logical(), complex(), and raw() each printed a zero-length vector of their own type. The hypothesis that survived is sharper than the one that was written down first.
Untyped pairlist emptiness collapses. Every other zero is a real node of its own type.
R Internals says there is only one object of type NILSXP, and it has no data. The constructor in memory.c is worth reading slowly:
It is a cons cell that points at itself in every direction, allocated before any other cons cell, with the reference count pinned and mutation forbidden. The write barrier refuses assignments into its fields. Empty hash buckets point at it. The empty formal list points at it. The end of every pairlist points at it. “No binding here,” “no attribute,” “no rest of this chain,” and “the user said NULL” are the same node because the Lisp tradition this evaluator comes from treats the empty list and nil as one object, and because having two of them would make every == R_NilValue pointer check a lie.
That is the sense in which Nil is special. Special does not mean “has a richer identity than a typed empty.” It means the runtime has exactly one, forever, and a large amount of C code compares pointers against it. A typed empty is special in a different way: it is allowed to be nothing of a particular kind. Programs should imitate the second kind. A zero that still has a type is a value you can pass through lapply, attach a name to, and refuse to confuse with “the argument was missing.”

title: 3  Three Empties
3  Three Empties
text:
3.2 Why list() refuses to collapse
The tempting explanation is dispatch. .S3PrimitiveGenerics and .internalGenerics are right there in the notebook, and they look like a reason. They are a reason that some operations on vectors are wired into the primitive table for speed. They are not why the empty list has its own node.
list() is a R’s user-facing list. One header plus a contiguous array of SEXP pointers, type VECSXP.generic vector. The manual’s description of VECSXP is a header, a length, a true length, and a block of SEXP pointers. Length zero is a legitimate block. It has to be, because the zero of the user-facing heterogeneous container has to remain that container:

typeof(list()) is "list", and length(list()) is 0
is.null(list()) is FALSE, which a huge amount of real code depends on
you can set names on it, grow it with [[<-, and hand it to lapply
an empty list with no class is still not NULL, so the OBJ bit and the class attribute stay out of the explanation

Pairlists follow the other rule because they are cons chains. The empty chain is nil. On current R, pairlist() is an R function: as.pairlist(list(...)). allocList(0) returns R_NilValue, which is why the empty call is Nil rather than a zero-length cons node. R kept that rule for the substrate — formals, attributes, the tail of a call — and grew a different empty for analysts.
alist() is the subtle one. It is also an R function, as.list(sys.call())[-1], so the arguments are not evaluated and the result is still a generic vector. Empty, it is another zero-length VECSXP, at its own address. The name “alist” is historical. The representation is the vector world’s.

title: 3  Three Empties
text:
3.3 Typed emptiness is a value
integer() is not “nothing.” It is a length-zero integer vector. Sum it, recycle it, bind it as a column, give it a class. character() is a length-zero STRSXP, which means a vector of CHARSXP pointers with no pointers in it. The R-level word is "character". The C-level word is STRSXP. The single string inside a character vector is the thing called CHARSXP, and you almost never hold one of those at R level. The notebook guessed STRSEXP. Close, and the distinction matters the moment you read a header.
numeric() is double() by another door. typeof(numeric()) is "double". There is no NUMSXP.
This is also why c() with no arguments is Nil rather than “an empty atomic vector of unknown type.” c() is the concatenator. Given nothing to concatenate and no type to inherit, it returns NULL. Given integers, it returns an integer vector. The empty call is the degenerate case of a function, not the zero of a type. integer() is the zero of a type. They answer different questions, and the dumps are the proof that R refuses to pretend they are the same question.

title: 3  Three Empties
text:
3.4 What people mean by “no scalars”
S took a shortcut that still defines the language. Chambers describes it in the 2020 R Journal piece: there were not enough hands to build a language with scalars and also vectors, and the Fortran libraries underneath already thought in arrays. So the low-level scalar work stayed on the other side of the interface, and R inherited a world in which 1L is an integer vector of length one. The scalar bit in the header is an optimization for that common case, not a new type.
Typed emptiness is the dual of that decision. If everything is a vector, the empty vector has to exist, per type, or “zero of these” collapses into “absence” and absence already has a resident. Nil is absence. integer() is a count of zero. Keeping them apart is one of the few places R is stricter than its reputation.

title: 4  Cons and Vectors
text:
4.1 A cons cell is three pointers
“Random access” sounds like a hardware claim. In this language it is an indexing claim. Both structures live on the heap, in the collector’s node pools. The C stack and the protection stack are real, and they are not where your list is stored.
Lisp’s cons is short for construct. A A heap node with a head, a tail, and an optional name. Pairlists and calls are chains of them.cons cell is one node:
A pairlist of length three is three heap nodes linked by CDR, and the last CDR is R_NilValue. Reaching element i walks i links. That cost is linear. Attributes are stored this way. Formals are stored this way. The manual is explicit that a LANGSXP, the type of a call, is a pairlist whose CAR is the function and whose CDR is the arguments, tags included when the caller named them.
You can see it in any classed object’s attribute dump. names and class are tags on a LISTSXP. The values hanging off those tags are ordinary vectors, often a STRSXP of length one whose single CHARSXP is in the string cache and has a ridiculous reference count because the cache is doing its job. The structure around them is still a linked list. R did not modernize that path. It stopped asking analysts to live on it.

title: 4  Cons and Vectors
section: 4.2 A generic vector is an array of pointers
text:
4.2 A generic vector is an array of pointers
A VECSXP is one header plus a contiguous block of SEXP pointers. Element i is data[i]. That is constant time. That is all “random access” means here. It does not mean the pairlist is on the stack, and it does not mean the vector is a C array of unboxed values. The pointers in a list refer to other nodes, which have their own headers, their own counts, their own possibility of being shared.
Atomic vectors are the unboxed case: an INTSXP really is a block of C ints, a REALSXP a block of doubles. A list is a block of pointers to values. Sharing a list and sharing an element of the list are different facts. That difference is why changing one column of a data frame does not have to copy the other columns. The vector of column pointers is the thing that gets duplicated. The untouched columns keep their addresses. Advanced R’s chapter on names and values is the patient version of this, with pictures.

title: 4  Cons and Vectors
text:
4.3 Demoted, not deleted
Early R was closer to Scheme. Implementing a GNU S pushed the pairlist inward and the vector outward. Chambers’ history in the R Journal article is the long version of that turn: an interface to Fortran arrays, a user language of expressions that return objects, and an implementation that grew a second, vector-shaped world on top of a cons-shaped evaluator.
What remains of the cons world at the surface:

pairlist() and as.pairlist(), which most code never needs
the occasional pairlist that leaks out of a primitive and gets coerced to a list on the way past
formals(), which returns a pairlist because that is what a closure’s formals are
attributes, which you manipulate with attr and attributes so you never have to walk the chain yourself
every call you quote, which is a LANGSXP and therefore a cons chain you are encouraged to treat as data

“R did not abandon cons; it demoted them to implementation substrate” is this split, said in one line. Analysts get vectors and generic vectors. The evaluator keeps cons cells for the sentences of the language and for the metadata hung on values. When a pairlist crosses into user code it is often promoted, because the user-facing sequence type won.
The terminology is scar tissue. In Lisp a list is a chain of conses. In R a list is a VECSXP, and the chain of conses is called a pairlist so that the two can coexist in one manual. If that naming bothers you, it should. It is the sound of two languages that refused to give up their word for the same idea.

title: 4  Cons and Vectors
section: 4.4 What you can see without a microscope
text:
4.4 What you can see without a microscope
typeof(quote(f(x = 1)))   # "language"  -> LANGSXP
typeof(formals(mean))     # often "pairlist"
typeof(list(a = 1))       # "list"      -> VECSXP
typeof(attributes(factor(1)))  # "pairlist" or NULL, and the class attribute is real
lobstr::ast() prints a call as a tree because the call is a tree of cons cells. lobstr::ref() on a list shows you the pointer array and then the children. The two pictures are the two worlds. Once you can see which world a given object is in, a surprising number of performance folktales become ordinary data-structure facts: walking a pairlist in a tight loop is a linked-list walk, growing a vector without the true-length trick is copying an array, and [[ on a list is an index, not a search.
The protection stack is the other “stack” worth a sentence, so it stops haunting the word. R’s C API requires callers to protect nodes they want to survive a garbage collection. That protection is a pointer stack in the runtime, described around the memory-allocator sections of the internals manual. It is bookkeeping for the collector. It is not the place pairlists live, and it is not an invitation to reason about user objects as stack-allocated values. User-visible SEXPs are heap nodes. Full stop.

title: 5  The Value Illusion
text:
5.1 From NAMED to a real count
Copy-on-modify feels like a magic trick because a 5 GB data frame can lose one cell and the machine does not blink. The feeling is accurate. The explanation is ordinary, once you are willing to look at three mechanisms that were built decades apart and happen to serve the same illusion.
The public rule: ordinary objects behave as values. Binding a new name does not copy. Modifying through one name does not change the other name. The private rule: nodes are shared until a write, and a write copies only when the reference count says someone else still cares.
That is The rule that a shared ordinary vector is duplicated before a write, so other names keep the old value.copy-on-modify. It is not a copy on every touch, and it is not mutation of a shared value. It is a copy at the moment a write would otherwise be visible through a second name.
Before R 4.0 the bit that answered “may I mutate this?” was NAMED, and it was a terrible counter. It went up to 2 and almost never came back down. A value that had ever been shared stayed “maybe shared” forever, so later writes copied even when every other holder had already gone away. Luke Tierney’s notes on reference counting are the design argument, written while the new scheme was still something you compiled in with SWITCH_TO_REFCNT. They are a historical document with a living conclusion. Read them as the motivation, then look at a modern dump: REF(n) is the count, and the macros in Defn.h increment and decrement it at the same assignments that maintain the generational write barrier.
The write barrier is the part worth understanding, because it explains why the bookkeeping is affordable. A generational collector has to notice when an old node grows a pointer to a young one, or the young one gets collected while the old one still needs it. Those assignment sites already existed. Reference counting hitchhiked on them: store a new pointer, increment the new target, decrement the old one. The value illusion is what that bookkeeping buys the user.
A few holders deliberately do not count. Tierney lists .Last.value, the left-hand side of a complex assignment, and some internal argument lists built with CONS_NR so that merely calling a function does not pin the arguments into permanent sharing. This is why a count is not a moral fact about your code. It is a census of whoever the runtime and the IDE have chosen to track.
The practical consequences, all visible from user level and spelled out in Advanced R:
Environments do not play this game. Assigning into an environment mutates the frame. duplicate1 in the runtime returns an environment unchanged, in the same group as Nil, symbols, external pointers, and weak references. The reference count still tells you how many names point at that environment. It does not trigger a duplicate-on-write of the bindings. Chambers says the contradiction on purpose, in S, R, and Data Science: an environment is accessed by reference, “which deliberately contradicts the usual non-reference semantics of S,” and the same computation “might have different results if that object was an environment on one hand or a list with the same elements corresponding to the same names on the other.” That is the warning the dumps are a photograph of. An environment with REF(11) is a popular handle, not a value that is about to be copied for your safety. The global environment is saturated and locked because it is part of the process.

title: 5  The Value Illusion
text:
x <- y shares. tracemem or lobstr::obj_addr will agree.
y[1] <- 0 on a shared atomic vector allocates a new vector for y.
Replacing one column of a data frame duplicates the list of columns and the one column you replaced. The other columns keep their addresses. That is the 5 GB frame that “copies” without copying 5 GB.
A count of 1 means the runtime believes you are the only holder, and a primitive is allowed to modify the node in place. This is a promise about the implementation, not a license to depend on in-place behavior in package code unless you are writing C and have checked the count yourself.

title: 5  The Value Illusion
section: 5.2 ALTREP is the same idea, one floor down
text:
5.2 ALTREP is the same idea, one floor down
Reference counting avoids copies of data you already materialized. A framework for giving an ordinary SEXPTYPE a different payload, such as a compact sequence or a deferred string.ALTREP avoids materializing the data.
The design note by Tierney, Becker, and Kalibera, ALTREP: Alternative Representations for R Objects, is the primary source, with the 2017 DSC slides and the 2018 tech note listed from developer.r-project.org. The goal is representational freedom under a stable SEXPTYPE. To existing C code an ALTREP integer still looks like an INTSXP. The payload can be something else:

a compact arithmetic sequence, so 1:1e9 does not allocate a billion integers
a deferred conversion of strings
a memory-mapped or distributed vector
metadata such as “sorted” or “no NAs,” so a later question can be answered without a scan
in the original sketch, even an alternative shape for environments

The abstract classes (ALTREP, ALTVEC, ALTINTEGER, ALTREAL, ALTSTRING, …) are fixed to the existing type tags. There is no user hierarchy of representations. A method can return a C NULL to mean “fall back to the ordinary protocol,” which is why the feature could land in a thirty-year-old interpreter. Dataptr_or_null is the polite question: give me the data if it is already here, and do not allocate if it is not. Extract_subset is how a slice of a compact sequence stays compact.
This is the same family of idea as a buffer protocol or a view: the type tag is the contract, the bytes are a choice. It is also why “I assigned 1:n and the memory graph did not move” is not evidence that R is reference-semantic. It is evidence that the sequence was never a pile of boxes to begin with. Force the payload — inspect is often enough, or any operation that needs a real data pointer — and the boxes appear.
The alt bit in the header is the flag. Combined with the allocation class, it tells you whether you are looking at a node that owns bytes or a node that knows how to produce them.

title: 5  The Value Illusion
text:
5.3 Promises are the calling convention
Arguments are not passed as values. They are passed as A delayed argument. An expression plus an environment, forced at most once, then remembered.promises: a PROMSXP holding the expression, the environment in which to evaluate it, and eventually the value. The manual states the lifecycle in one sentence. Once the promise has been forced, the environment pointer is set to NULL and the value is remembered. Force-once. After that, the argument is just a value with a history.
That is why the public phrase “pass by value” is a description of the illusion, not of the calling convention. The convention is: pass by promise, share until a write, duplicate if the count says the write would leak. Laziness here is not Haskell’s laziness. Haskell delays evaluation to keep expressions referentially transparent and to permit infinite structures. R delays evaluation so that a plot can use the expression you typed as a label, so that a default argument can mention another argument, and so that non-standard evaluation has something to capture. The cost is evaluation-order surprises. The benefit is the part of the REPL that feels like talking.
Specials and builtins are the exception that proves the rule, and they get their own section in Chapter 6. A special does not even build the promises. It receives the arguments raw.

title: 5  The Value Illusion
section: 5.4 <<- is mutation with the receiver left blank
text:
5.4 <<- is mutation with the receiver left blank
The discomfort with <<-, set next to the comfort with environments, is not hypocrisy once you separate mutation from finding the thing you mutate.
<<- walks the enclosure chain, the same walk a free variable uses on the way out, and assigns into the first binding it finds, or into the global environment if it finds none. The target depends on who enclosed the function. Move the function, wrap it, local() it, put it in a package namespace, and the walk can land somewhere else. The mutation is real. The receiver is implicit. That is a fragile API even when the memory model is doing exactly what it was asked.
An explicit environment, or an R6 object, or an S7 object whose parent is class_environment, names the receiver. Aliases see the same mutation because identity is the point. You can pass the handle, fake it in a test, and refuse to let a helper go fishing in its parents. Both techniques modify shared state. One of them puts the shared state in the signature.
The social rule “never use <<-” is a documentation rule that got promoted to a moral one. The memory-model rule underneath it is better: do not mutate through a search. If identity matters, hold the object. If identity does not matter, return a value and let copy-on-modify do its job.
Haskell’s ST monad is the typed version of the same instinct. The paper is Launchbury and Peyton Jones, “Lazy Functional State Threads” (POPL 1994). The encapsulation is not a runtime fence. It is the rank-2 type of runST, roughly “for all states s, an ST s a computation yields an a.” A mutable reference that mentions s cannot escape, so the outside world still sees a pure function. The weaker type ST s a -> a would not do that job. R can imitate the pattern — scratch environment in, list or S7 value out — and has no type system that can enforce the boundary. The fence is a convention you write down. Package code that returns the handle by accident has broken the fence, and nothing in the language will clear its throat.

title: 5  The Value Illusion
text:
5.5 What the illusion is for
The illusion is for reasoning. A function that takes a data frame and returns a data frame can be read as a transformation of a value, even though the columns you did not touch are shared and the sequence you did not expand is still compact. Tests can compare values. Pipes can be reread. Names do not secretly observe each other’s later assignments.
The illusion is a lie for exactly the objects where observation is the feature: environments, external pointers, weak references, and reference classes built on top of them. Chambers’ principles say everything is an object and everything that happens is a function call. They do not say every object has value semantics. The dumps are where you learn which objects opted out. Designing as if they all opted in, or as if none of them did, is how packages get either haunted state or tragic performance.

title: 6  In Context
text:
6.1 Builtins and specials
A lot of SEXP types feel mythical until the right expression manufactures one. Absence from a typical script is not absence from the type system. The notebook kept bumping into this, and it is worth walking type by type with the context that makes each one show up.
typeof(sum) is "builtin". typeof([) is "special". typeof({) is "special". typeof(function() NULL) is "closure". The nodes are BUILTINSXP, SPECIALSXP, and CLOSXP. They are easy to miss because printing them shows .Primitive("sum") or the source of the closure, and because you rarely inspect the function rather than the value it returned.
The semantic difference is the old Lisp split between an applicative function and a form that receives code. A builtin evaluates its arguments, then receives the values. A special does not. [, if, {, &&, ||, function, quote, and <- have to be specials, because evaluating everything first would destroy the construct. `&&` must not touch the right-hand side when the left-hand side is false. function must not evaluate the body at definition time. The internals manual calls these out as special primitives.
Closures are the third kind: formals (a pairlist), body (usually a LANGSXP), and enclosing environment. That triple is what inspect prints under FORMALS, BODY, and CLOENV. An S7 class is one of these. The notebook’s new_class() dump is a CLOSXP with a class attribute of c("S7_class", "S7_object") and a pile of metadata — name, parent, properties, validator, constructor — hanging off the attribute pairlist. The constructor you call is a function. The class object is that function, plus attributes. That is a very R solution: reuse the closure node you already have, and hang the dictionary off the side.

title: 6  In Context
section: 6.2 Objects, factors, and the integer64 lie
text:
6.2 Objects, factors, and the integer64 lie
Two different words got called “object,” and the confusion is reasonable.
is.object(x) answers the OBJ bit, which the header comment defines as “does this have a class attribute?” Adding a class sets the bit. Removing the class clears it. A factor is an INTSXP with a levels attribute and class = "factor". The bit is set. typeof stays "integer". OBJSXP is a different question: type code 25, the node used when an S4 or S7 object is not itself a simple vector or function. An S4 object that does carry vector data keeps that vector’s SEXPTYPE and sets a separate S4 bit in gp. isS4() reads that bit. It does not ask whether the type code is 25. The notebook’s S7 instance, after @p <- "aaa", is type 25. The factor never was.
Factors feel “more low-level” because base R and the C API know them intimately: modeling code, tabulation, printing, levels<- as a primitive generic. The representation pattern is still the S3 pattern. Historically they had their own SEXP types, codes 11 and 12, and those were withdrawn. The withdrawal is the tell. R decided that “integer plus attributes” was enough type system for factors, and then lived with the consequences.
bit64::integer64() is the same pattern with the costume showing. typeof is "double". Inspect shows a REALSXP with OBJ and ATT, and a class string "integer64". A double is 64 bits wide, so the package stores a 64-bit integer in the payload a double would have used and lies, politely, at the class layer. S3 as a reinterpretation of storage is half of R’s power. You can ship a new semantic type without a new SEXPTYPE, which is why the set of SEXPTYPEs can stay frozen. It is also half of R’s pain. Every function that forgets to be generic will treat the payload as what it physically is. mean of an integer64 without a method is a nonsense double. The class is law. The SEXPTYPE is physics. Code that only knows physics will enforce physics.
S7::class_any is a useful decoy. Inspect shows a length-zero VECSXP with class "S7_any". It is not an S7 class constructor, and it is not an OBJSXP. It is a base-type object used as a property constraint meaning “anything.” The slot exists so that a property can name its admitted type. Leaving it at class_any is a choice, and Chapter 12 argues it is usually the wrong one.

title: 6  In Context
text:
6.3 Promises, dots, and byte code
You meet a PROMSXP by forcing the issue: delayedAssign, or inspecting a formal while a call is live and the argument has not been touched. Dots are DOTSXP, a pairlist of promises bound to .... Byte code is BCODESXP. The compiler produces it, package loading produces it, and in the S7 dumps the parent class S7_object already has a byte-coded body because the package was built with the compiler on. You did not ask for byte code. You asked for S7, and the namespace handed you a compiled closure.
None of these require a debugger if you know which expression allocates them. They do require you to stop expecting inspect(1L) to introduce you to the whole zoo. The zoo comes to you when evaluation, compilation, or a package constructor needs it.

title: 6  In Context
text:
6.4 External pointers and weak references
These two get conflated because both smell like “systems programming,” and they answer different questions.









External pointer
Weak reference




Type
EXTPTRSXP
WEAKREFSXP


Manual’s picture
a pointer, a protected R object, and a tag
a length-4 vector: key, value, finalizer, next


Job
name a foreign resource
remember a value only while the key is alive


Death
a finalizer can run when the pointer is collected
when the key dies, the weak reference clears and does not keep the key alive



An external pointer is how an R object owns a GDAL dataset, a database connection, a C++ instance. The R object is the handle you can name, protect, and finalize. The bytes live in someone else’s allocator. reg.finalizer is the base-R hook. It registers a function to run after the key has been found unmarked, at a safe point following collection, once. It does not run at the instant the last binding disappears, and the help page is blunt that arbitrary R from a finalizer has already caused trouble. It accepts environments and external pointers, not lists. That is the interface principle from Chambers, made concrete: talking to other languages includes talking about their lifetimes.
A weak reference is a cache that does not create a leak. The key is an environment or an external pointer (or NULL). The value is what you wanted to remember. The collector is allowed to forget the value when the key is otherwise unreachable. Memoisation tables and package registries use this so that “I have seen this object” does not become “I will keep this object forever.”
The user’s complaint is correct and worth keeping. The C type being real is not the same thing as a base constructor you can teach to a beginner. rlang::new_weakref is a language-level wrapper. typeof on its result is "weakref", so once you hold one, R will admit the type exists. Building one by hand is a C or package job. reg.finalizer is the piece base actually exports for the neighboring problem. A lot of “tidyverse primitives” have this shape: the runtime grew the capability, and a package grew the API. ALTREP classes, a comfortable restart surface, and weak maps all sit in that gap. Internals are not the standard library. Pretending they are is how people tell you the feature “already exists” when what exists is a struct.

title: 6  In Context
section: 6.5 S7 values and R6 handles, at the level of nodes
text:
6.5 S7 values and R6 handles, at the level of nodes
This is the identity fork, photographed.
An S7 class object is a CLOSXP. Calling it allocates an instance. In the notebook the instance is an OBJSXP whose attributes carry the class string and a pointer back at the class. Properties live in that structure. @p <- went through a replacement function and the address changed. Same physics as df$x <- on a data frame: value semantics, copy-on-modify, a new node for the modified object. The class object itself is shared. Instances point back at it. Dispatch is generic functions, not messages stored in the instance.
An R6 generator is an ENVSXP. The dump is a guided tour of a mutable dictionary: a hash table, bindings for classname and public_fields, closures whose enclosing environment is the generator itself, a clone method whose body builds new environments and remaps closures into them, lockEnvironment, reg.finalizer wired to $finalize, and the famous .__enclos_env__ chain. Methods are closures closed over the object environment. That is the Scheme model of an object, shipped as a package. $foo <- does not change the address. Cloning is an explicit walk. The giant paste in the notebook is the clone machinery’s source, seen from the inside, and it is allowed to be ugly. It is doing something the value world gets for free.
S7’s experimental class_environment is the admission that the class machinery and the identity regime are separable. You can ask for S7’s properties and validators on environment physics. The documentation marks it dangerous because it is dangerous: you have opted out of the value illusion while keeping a syntax that looks like the illusion. Use it when you mean a handle. Do not use it because an environment seemed like a convenient list.

title: 6  In Context
section: 6.6 What the physics does not decide
text:
6.6 What the physics does not decide
Knowing that an instance is an OBJSXP does not tell you whether color should be a class. It tells you that if you make it an S7 value, property replacement will behave like data-frame replacement, and if you make it an R6 object, property replacement will behave like environment assignment. The physics constrains the promises you can keep. The vocabulary is still your job. That is the hinge into the second half of the book.

title: 7  Signals
text:
7.1 Three moves, not one
The comment in the notebook is the right complaint, and it is more precise than it felt at the time.
R’s conditions are S3 objects sitting on a signaling mechanism that can run a handler while the stack is still alive, muffle a warning, or invoke a restart. The culture around them is an exception culture: stop, tryCatch, unwind, maybe wrap the message in a new class and stop again. Both facilities are real. One of them is taught. The other is how robust software actually wants to talk.
Kent Pitman’s retrospective on condition handling separates what most languages glue together. The Common Lisp HyperSpec states the mechanism in chapter 9. Compressed:
tryCatch does a narrower thing. It establishes an exiting handler. The stack unwinds to the catch, and then your function runs. Whatever the callee might have done to fix the problem and continue is gone. That is the right tool when the policy really is “abandon this attempt.” It is the wrong default when the policy is “hear about this and decide.”
withCallingHandlers establishes a calling handler. It runs on the live stack. withRestarts and invokeRestart are the resume mechanism, and they are base R, not a package invention. signalCondition is the low-level signal. Warnings and messages are conditions that happen to have default handlers installed by the runtime: print something, and in the warning case continue. tryCatch on a warning is you replacing that policy with an unwind. Sometimes you want that. Often you wanted to muffle, collect, or re-signal.
The R implementation of the split is older than the tidyverse wrappers. Robert Gentleman and Luke Tierney wrote A Prototype of a Condition System for R and distinguished exiting handlers from calling handlers there. Advanced R’s conditions chapter is the practical map, including the class hierarchy (condition → error / warning / message, and your subclasses under those). It also says, honestly, that restarts are out of its scope. The help pages for withRestarts and tryCatch are the reference for the base mechanism. rlang::try_fetch() is the current “handler that can return a value” spelling, and the cnd_ constructors are how you build the objects without hand-rolled structure() calls. None of this is obscure because it is weak. It is obscure because the first page of search results says tryCatch.

title: 7  Signals
text:
Signal. Name a situation by allocating an object, not by throwing a string.
Handle. Decide policy while the stack that signaled is still there. A handler can repair, muffle, log, or decline.
Restart. Offer a named way to resume. invokeRestart transfers control to a restart the signaler, or someone above the signaler, established for this purpose.

title: 7  Signals
text:
7.2 Catching a 500 to throw a 500
The failure mode is a layering mistake.
An HTTP library that sees status 500 has learned a fact. The fact wants a class: the status, the URL, the body, the request id. That class is the signal, or it is the value you return if you have chosen errors-as-values for this boundary. What the application does about it is a different function, living in a different place.







Layer
Job




Library boundary
Signal a classed condition, or return a result value, with enough structure to branch on


Policy boundary
withCallingHandlers or try_fetch map that class onto a recovery, a richer condition, or a logged warning


Application boundary
Abort, retry, prompt, or degrade, by invoking a restart or by returning



Catching an httr2 error solely to stop() with a new message throws away the class the library already gave you and forces every caller to parse text. Re-signaling a richer condition, with the original as the parent, is a different act: you are translating a transport fact into a domain fact. The class is the point of the translation. The string is for the human at the host.
Parent classes matter here. A handler for http_error can sit above a handler for http_error_500. A handler for error is the wide net. S3 dispatch on the condition’s class is the “native method dispatch” the comment was reaching for. It works. It works only if someone signals a class worth dispatching on, and only if the handler is registered where the stack still has the context to use it.

title: 7  Signals
section: 7.3 Errors as values are a neighboring door
text:
7.3 Errors as values are a neighboring door
Rust’s Result, purrr’s safely, and a validator that returns a failure value instead of signaling are a different design with the same taste. The failure is data. The caller branches on it with ordinary control flow. There is no stack discipline to get right, and there is also no way for a caller three frames up to establish a restart the callee can invoke. You chose an explicit return channel over a signal channel.
R can do both, which means a package has to pick. One effect story per boundary. Fatal stop for programmer errors and invariant failures. Classed signals for situations a caller might plausibly handle. Result values when the failure is an ordinary outcome of the domain (“this address did not geocode”) and you do not want it traveling by a side channel. Mixing all three in one function, plus a cat() of the URL for good measure, is how an API feels schizophrenic.
S7 validators that return character vectors of problems are already in the errors-as-values family. They are not a condition system. They are a parse step. Use them at construction. Use conditions for what happens later, when a well-built value meets a world that can still say no.

title: 7  Signals
text:
7.4 Streams, and the C leak
PowerShell’s output streams are the cleanest picture of what a condition system is for, even though the substrate is different. The official list is in about_Output_Streams:

The win is orthogonal channels. A function can return a value and warn and describe what it is doing, and the caller decides what to keep. PowerShell’s redirection (3>&1, and the rules in about_Redirection) makes that a shell feature. R makes it a handler feature. The idea is the same: side-channel meaning is structured, and the host picks it up at the edge.
Two R-specific cuts.
Warnings and messages are already conditions, so they can be muffled, collected, promoted to errors (options(warn = 2) is the blunt version), or given a class and a handler. cli output that goes through the condition-aware UI is in this world. A hand-rolled cat() is not. Text on the console cannot be dispatched. It can only be captured, and capture is a miserable API.
C stdout and stderr are a second console that R’s condition system does not own. A .Call that printfs has stepped outside the protocol. Robust packages treat that as a bug unless the foreign chatter is caught and re-signaled as a condition, or explicitly documented as a debug leak. The interface principle cuts both ways. You may call C. C does not get to talk to your user behind the language’s back.

title: 7  Signals
text:
7.5 A package doctrine
Small enough to stick on the wall:

Return values for success. Type them.
Signal classed conditions for everything a caller might route.
Prefer calling handlers and try_fetch at library boundaries; use tryCatch when you truly mean “this attempt is over.”
Establish restarts where a caller could plausibly resume: skip this record, use this default, retry with this credential.
Put narration and progress in cli or in messages, behind a preference.
Do not cat() a situation you could signal.
If C talks, wrap the talk.

This is the functional-core idea applied to communication. The core returns a value or signals an object. The shell — the handler, the option, the CLI flag, the IDE — decides what the human sees. The next chapters are about why R grew a core that will not enforce any of this, and why that is survivable.

title: 8  Lineage
text:
8.1 Three principles, visible from the first blackboard
R’s oddness is not an accident that later programmers failed to clean up. It is a hybrid engineered for interactive data analysis, afterwards asked to carry production systems. The sophistication of the REPL and the friction of a hardened package are the same design, seen from two ends.
In a 2016 book Chambers claimed the design of R can be summarized in three principles. He repeated them, with the history attached, in S, R, and Data Science (The R Journal, 2020). The wording there:
He is careful about the chronology. The principles were not invented late as a brand. They are “broadly visible from the first version of S.” The May 1976 sketch he reprints is an interface: a Fortran subroutine on one side, an S object in, an S object out. Assignment is a function. Modeling returns an object. The user language looks like scientific expressions because the likely users were comfortable with scientific expressions, and because real analyses get tree-shaped fast. A colleague’s suggestion of a shell of pipes was considered and declined. Pipes came back, decades later, as syntax over the function-call principle. They did not replace it.
The scalar decision is in the same essay. S had no scalar types distinct from general objects, partly because the Fortran library already managed arrays, partly because there were not enough programmers to build a second language underneath. “The intention was that low-level computations depending on these would be done through the interface to Fortran.” You are still living in that intention every time 1 is a vector.
Extending R (Chapman and Hall/CRC, 2016) is the book the article cites for the principles, pages 4–11. The article is the piece you can actually open in a browser. Prefer it when you want the history; prefer the book when you want the design worked out as a programming model.

title: 8  Lineage
text:
objects: Everything that exists in R is an object.
functions: Everything that happens in R is a function call.
interfaces: Interfaces to other languages are a part of R.

title: 8  Lineage
section: 8.2 A Scheme engine asked to host S
text:
8.2 A Scheme engine asked to host S
Ihaka and Gentleman’s 1996 paper in the Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics introduces R as a language for data analysis and graphics, in the S tradition, with lexical scope taken seriously. The R Language Definition states the compromise in the introduction:

The language syntax has a superficial similarity with C, but the semantics are of the FPL (functional programming language) variety with stronger affinities with Lisp and APL. In particular, it allows “computing on the language.”

Chapter 6 of the same manual is the part to sit with. R “presents a friendlier interface to programming than Lisp does, at least to someone used to mathematical formulas and C-like control structures, but the engine is really very Lisp-like.” Calls are data. You can quote them, rearrange them, and eval them. Plot labels, model formulas, and tidy evaluation are applications of that fact. They are not a macro system bolted on later.

Luke Tierney’s Lisp-Stat (Wiley, 1990) is a statistical environment built in Lisp, with dynamic graphics and objects, and Tierney later did an enormous share of R’s runtime: the generational collector, the compiler, reference counting, ALTREP. Influence is not identity. R is not Lisp-Stat with different syntax. The accurate claim is smaller. The evaluator R shipped with is Scheme-descended, and the person who then made that evaluator industrially serious had already built a Lisp for statistics. You can feel both facts in the dumps. You should not cite them as one fact.

title: 8  Lineage
text:
8.3 What the corpus said
Morandat, Hill, Osvald, and Vitek, Evaluating the Design of the R Language (ECOOP 2012), looked at the language the way language researchers look at a language: static and dynamic analysis of a large corpus. Their abstract is the quote to keep. R “combines lazy functional features and object-oriented programming. This rather unlikely linguistic cocktail would probably never have been prepared by computer scientists, yet the language has become surprisingly popular.”
The paper’s lasting usefulness is the permission it gives you to treat the cocktail as a design you can evaluate, not as weather. Lazy promises, vectorization, a functional core, imperative locals, more than one object system, reflection into the implementation: users pick among these ad hoc, because the language permits all of them. That finding is still true, and it is the reason a package has to have an opinion. The language will not supply one.

title: 8  Lineage
section: 8.4 Interfaces, including the ones that hurt
text:
8.4 Interfaces, including the ones that hurt
The third Chambers principle is why .Call, Fortran, C++, Arrow, GDAL, and databases do not feel like foreign-function trivia in R. They feel like the original blackboard. The external pointer and the finalizer are the modern picture of that 1976 rectangle: something outside, an object on the way in, an object on the way out, and a question about who frees the memory.
It is also why a printf inside that rectangle is a design bug rather than a logging strategy. The interface was supposed to exchange objects. Text on a C stream is a second language the caller did not agree to parse. Chapter 7 already made this point from the condition side. From the historical side it is the same point. The interface is part of the language, so the interface has to speak the language.

title: 8  Lineage
section: 8.5 A clash you can stop apologizing for
text:
8.5 A clash you can stop apologizing for
C-like syntax, Lisp-like engine, Fortran-like data, statistical missingness, generic functions, and a reference-counted value illusion. None of these is a dialect you can subtract and still have R. The work is to know which one is speaking in a given line of code.
A LANGSXP is the Lisp engine. A REALSXP is the Fortran data. An ENVSXP is the Scheme closure’s home, and also R6’s home. A promise is the calling convention that makes the REPL feel telepathic. NA is the statistical practice, built into the type rather than wrapped around it. REF is the modern implementation earning the value illusion the syntax has always sold. When a design argument in your package feels confused, it is often because two of these are being asked to answer the same question. Split the question. The lineage tells you which voice answers which one.

title: 9  The REPL, Then the Contract
text:
9.1 What the conversation is good at
The language definition describes the intended first experience in passing, and it is the whole product philosophy:
That ladder — expression, function, package — is the honest path. It is also why a person who wants illegal states to be unrepresentable feels like they are fighting the grain. They are. The grain is a conversation. Contracts are what you write down when the conversation has discovered a thing worth keeping.
Interactive data work wants:
Features that serve that ladder are easy to mistake for sloppiness. Promises let a plotting function capture the expression you wrote. Attributes let a vector grow a class without a new runtime type. The search path lets a new package’s verbs appear in the conversation. Recycling and permissive coercion let a one-liner survive contact with a column that is almost the right shape. NA lets a summary skip missing measurements without a parallel Option type. Non-standard evaluation lets a modeling formula look like the thing a statistician would write on paper.
Morandat and colleagues described this lifecycle as the context in which the linguistic cocktail makes sense. Take the lifecycle away and a lot of R looks indefensible. Leave it in place and the language looks like a tool that knows what the first hour of analysis is.

title: 9  The REPL, Then the Contract
section: 9.2 What the conversation will not do for you
text:
9.2 What the conversation will not do for you
The same features are anti-features for “schema at the boundary,” until you impose a discipline above the language.
A promise will evaluate in a surprising environment if you capture it and force it later. A class attribute will be ignored by any function that is not generic. The search path will resolve a name to whatever was attached last. Coercion will add a factor level you did not mean, or drop one. NA will flow through a logical test and return NA, and if (NA) will complain, and somewhere in that pair of behaviors a bug will hide for a year. None of this is a reason to refuse the REPL. It is a reason to treat the REPL as the place you discover the concept, and the package as the place you stop the concept from leaking.
The sequence that matches the ladder, said as advice:

Explore with the dynamic machine. Dirty data, wrong types, one-off plots, inspect when a result is absurd.
Notice the nouns that kept coming back, and the verbs you repeated.
Parse those nouns at the boundary. Constructors that refuse junk. format methods that make the meaning obvious.
Package the verbs. Generics where a stranger should be able to add a method. A handle only where identity is the feature.

Step 2 is the part people skip, and then step 3 becomes ceremony around the wrong nouns. The low-level session this book came from was step 1 aimed at the language itself. That is allowed. Most days step 1 is aimed at a file full of addresses.

title: 9  The REPL, Then the Contract
section: 9.3 Why Python and JavaScript feel more direct
text:
9.3 Why Python and JavaScript feel more direct
They default to named objects with methods. The habit “there is a class for this” is ambient, so the path from a domain noun to a bundle of behavior is short. You still do not get real contracts until you add something like Pydantic or Zod. The object was never the contract. It was a place to put methods. The contract arrives when construction parses.
R’s ambient habit is “there is a function for this,” and a class is optional metadata on a vector. The path from a domain noun to a defended value is longer, because you are building the noun out of a vector, a class attribute, and a constructor the language considers optional. The reward, when someone actually does it, is an API that composes. A request is a value. A plot specification is a value. A data frame is a relation. Verbs take these and return these. The user interface is the vocabulary.
This is a personal preference and also a technical one. Dislike of message-passing as a default is compatible with respecting what that default buys: one obvious place to look for behavior. R asks you to look in the verbs, which is wonderful when the verbs are curated and miserable when every package invents a private dialect. Curation is the price of the preference. Chapter 10 is about paying it on purpose.

title: 9  The REPL, Then the Contract
section: 9.4 Where R wins on the merits
text:
9.4 Where R wins on the merits
A few comparisons, kept specific so they do not turn into team sports.
httr2. A request is a value you build with a pipe of functions: URL, headers, body, authentication, then perform. The help page calls it an S3 list of class httr2_request (request()), and the introductory vignette shows the pipe. Errors are classed. The perform step is the edge where the value meets the network. This is the functional core and the imperative shell in one pipeline, and it is pleasant in a way object-graphs of HTTP clients often are not. You can see the request. You can print it before you send it. Printing is part of the design.
ellmer. A conversation with a model is a session you hold. The chat objects are R6, which is the right physics: turns accumulate, so identity is the feature. The operations on that handle are a small vocabulary: send a turn, register a tool, extract a typed value. The package site is the reference, and it points retrieval at ragnar rather than pretending the chat object is a framework. A conversation has identity, so a handle is the honest representation. The design win over a large agent framework is the size of the vocabulary and the refusal to hide the request. Compare that with LangChain-style graphs when you want a lesson in what “more objects” does to a domain that wanted a few verbs. The lesson is not that Python cannot be clear. It is that a framework can spend its complexity budget on the wrong axis.
ggplot2. Wilkinson’s Grammar of Graphics (Springer, 2005) gave the field a vocabulary. Wickham’s layered grammar is explicit that it is not that book unchanged: the components are arranged differently, the defaults differ, and the grammar is embedded in a programming language. You can dislike using ggplot2 and still recognize the move. A plot is a specification, a value, built by composing layers. It is not a scene graph you mutate. Formulas in modeling packages are the older version of the same move. R’s frameworks, when they work, look like grammars.
Tidy data and verbs. Once a data frame is a relation with a convention for rows and columns, a whole ecology of verbs can share it. The win is the shared noun, not any single package. A new verb can be written without inheriting from a table class. That is open dispatch as an industry structure, and it is the subject of the next chapter.

title: 9  The REPL, Then the Contract
text:
9.5 The nag
Python nags you early, with objects. You still need a schema library before the nag means “invalid states are unrepresentable.” R nags you late, with stopifnot scattered through helpers and with users who received a list and had to guess. Unless the package treats the contract as the product.
The REPL is not a betrayal of that product. It is how you find out which contracts are worth writing. The difficult part is that the language will never force the transition. You can stay in the conversation forever. Production R is the decision to leave the conversation in the places where the concept has stabilized, and to keep the conversation available everywhere it has not.
