title: 10  Open Verbs
text:
10.1 Generic functions
Decapsulating methods is a bet that a domain is an algebra. The verbs are the operations. The types are the elements they operate on. Extensibility means a new element can join an old operation, or a new operation can be defined on old elements, without anyone opening the type and adding a method to its private table.
R made that bet early, because statistics is full of operations that apply to more than one kind of thing: print, plot, summary, predict, coef, [. A model object does not contain the verb predict. The verb exists, and methods attach to it. Rust made a related bet for different reasons, and the resemblance is real if you do not sand off the parts that do not resemble.
In the generic-function tradition, the operation is a function and the method is chosen from the arguments. CLOS is the carefully designed version: multi-argument dispatch, method combinations, classes that do not own their behavior. S3 is the casually designed version that won: a naming convention, a search along the class vector, first-argument dispatch unless you reach for something richer. S4 adds formality and multiple dispatch. S7 keeps S3’s compatibility and adds a class and property model worth using. Advanced R’s object-oriented chapter sorts these without pretending they are one system.
The user’s daily experience of the bet:
Message-passing inverts the sentence. obj.predict() asks the object which method to run. Discovery is “what does this object know?” Extension is subclassing, wrapping, or patching. Python and JavaScript made this the default and it fits simulation-shaped problems: widgets, game entities, documents with a long identity, ORMs whose rows really are handles. It fits data work only after you build a second, functional layer on top and try not to talk about it.
R has both, and the culture never fully picked. R6 and reference classes are the message-passing wing. S3/S4/S7 are the generic-function wing. The winning user interfaces in statistics and in the tidyverse are still verb(noun) or noun |> verb(). $ exists. It is not a moral failure to use it on a handle. It is a clue that you have built a handle.

title: 10  Open Verbs
text:
a new package implements format.my_class and the console changes
a new package implements predict.my_model and old code starts working
nobody subclasses the original type
the verb stays a function, so it can sit in a pipe, a script, or a shell

title: 10  Open Verbs
text:
10.2 What Rust actually shares
Rust methods are sugar over functions. value.method(args) is Type::method(value, args) or Trait::method(value, args). There are two places a method can come from:

an inherent impl Type block, which is closed: only the crate that owns the type adds these
a trait implementation, which is open in a controlled way: other crates can implement the trait for their own types

The traits chapter of the Rust book is the mechanism. The API guidelines are stricter than the folklore: a function with a clear receiver should be a method. The case for a free function is narrow (a smart pointer should not grow inherent methods that look like methods of the inner type). Trait methods are still methods. What resembles R is the open impl: another crate can implement Display for its own type, under the orphan rules, without editing the original module. Ownership and lifetimes have no R equivalent, and pretending otherwise is how the comparison gets cute and then wrong. The comparison that holds is the shape of the code you read. Types are the backbone. Dispatch is a property of the operation. A new type can join Display, or predict, without inheriting the original type.
Rust’s orphan rules are the part R deliberately does not have. A trait implementation has to be coherent: you cannot have two crates each defining Display for the same foreign type and then wonder which one runs. R will happily let the next attached package mask a method, and UseMethod will pick whatever is found first on the search path. That is the extensibility and the footgun in one rule. Packages manage it with conventions, imports, and a refusal to define methods for classes they do not own unless that is the whole point of the package. The footgun is not an argument against open verbs. It is an argument for a curated vocabulary, which is the same argument the naming section already made.

title: 10  Open Verbs
section: 10.3 Naming as the module system you actually use
text:
10.3 Naming as the module system you actually use
Thinking in functions and shell-like procedures matches how you navigate a codebase under this bet.

api_config_new, api_client_fetch, color_brightness
check_*, as_*, format_*, req_*
Rust’s module::function

The prefix is the module. The package namespace is the fence. IDE navigation is symbol search over a vocabulary you chose, which is the same muscle as a good CLI. Encapsulation, in this style, means three things and refuses a fourth:

semantic: illegal states do not parse
nominal: the names are stable and the namespace is real
disciplinary: effects and handles are obvious in the signature
not: every verb hides behind self.

Dot-driven objects optimize for one blob of state with a toolbox attached. Function-and-type systems optimize for pipelines, scripts, and verbs that apply to more than one noun. Data work is the second shape. So are HTTP clients, tool-using model loops, and compilers. When an R codebase feels like Java with the classes rubbed off, it is usually because the verbs were never written down as verbs. The methods exist, scattered across files named after nouns, and the user interface is whatever you discover by typing $ and waiting.

title: 10  Open Verbs
text:
10.4 Algebras, not simulations
The cold version of the strength:
A simulation asks “what does this thing do next?” An algebra asks “what operations exist on these things, and which laws do they obey?” R’s generic functions are a bet on the second question. So are Rust traits, CLOS generic functions, and type classes in Haskell. Python’s classes are a bet on the first, with protocols and functools.singledispatch as the escape hatches for people who wanted the second bet after all.
Your preference is not anti-object. It is objects as a facade over a functional surface. Types carry meaning. Generics carry extensibility. Functions are what humans, pipes, and shells invoke. That is a coherent production style. It is one of the real reasons to stay in R when the alternative is an object graph that can do anything and explains nothing.
The style has a failure mode worth naming. A vocabulary nobody curates becomes a junk drawer of verbs: three ways to say “fetch,” methods defined for classes the package does not own, generics with a single method that should have been a function. Open dispatch is valuable when there is a second implementation in sight, or a stranger who might write one. A private function is a fine verb. Not everything has to dispatch. The test is whether a new noun should be able to join without editing the call sites. If yes, write the generic. If no, write the function and keep the name clean.

title: 11  Where State Lives
text:
11.1 Four questions
Statefulness is fine. Undeclared statefulness is what bites. Picking a container is picking where identity, validation, and lifetime live, and the runtime has already limited the menu. You do not invent a third physics. You choose a value or a handle, and you say so in the type.
Ask them in order.

title: 11  Where State Lives
text:
Does anyone need to observe mutation of the same object? An open connection, a token that refreshes, a cache, a progress meter, a conversation. Yes means a An object whose identity is part of the API. Aliases observe the same evolving state.reference owner: an environment, an R6 object, an external pointer, or an S7 class that has deliberately chosen environment physics. No means a value. Lists, S3 objects, and ordinary S7 objects are values. Copy-on-modify is the physics, whether you think about it or not.
Is this a domain fact or a process capability? Config, enums, colors, response schemas, and parsed documents are facts. They want to be values, because you want to compare them, print them, and put them in tests. “Talk to this API,” “hold this socket,” “retry with backoff” are capabilities. They want a handle that owns or receives values.
Who owns the lifetime? Process-wide defaults belong in a small package environment or in options(), documented, and treated as defaults rather than as the real API. Per session, per test, per request: construct the value or the handle and pass it. Hidden <<- into a parent the caller cannot name is how a helper becomes a seance.
Where do the contracts live? This is not “S7 or S3 depending on how serious you are.” Illegal states should be unrepresentable either way. The question is whether the contract is a ritual you maintain (new_*, validate_*, as_*, format_*) or a structure the object carries (S7 properties, validators, generics). Chapter 12 takes that fork. It does not weaken question 1.

title: 11  Where State Lives
text:
11.2 A concrete map
The API-shaped version, because it keeps coming up:








Thing
Container
Why




api_config: base URL, timeouts, auth material, enums
S7 or S3 value
A snapshot. Cheap to compare. Easy to build in a test. No identity.


api_client: request factory, token refresh, rate limit
R6, an environment, or a thin handle around httr2
Identity matters. The token you refresh is the token the next call must see.


Package default config
Locked package environment, or options()
Bootstrapping. Override by argument, not by a global write in the hot path.


Call-site wiring
Pass the client in
Tests inject fakes. Scripts inject the real handle.



config   : value     what is true
client   : handle    what can act
functions: take the handle, and take config overrides as values
package environment: defaults and registries only
The anti-pattern is one class that is both the config record and the live session. You then either mutate a thing that prints like a value, or you copy a thing that was supposed to be a handle and wonder why the refresh did not stick. The physics will not save you from that confusion. It will obey whichever choice you accidentally made.
Gary Bernhardt’s Boundaries talk (SCNA 2012) and his screencast Functional Core, Imperative Shell name the larger shape: a core that decides on values, a shell that performs effects. In R the core is values and verbs. The shell is the handle, the options() read at the edge, the handler that decides how a condition is shown. The split is not a style for people who dislike objects. It is a rule for where objects with identity are allowed to stand.

title: 11  Where State Lives
section: 11.3 Dependency injection without the enterprise voice
text:
11.3 Dependency injection without the enterprise voice
Passing the client is dependency injection. You do not need a container framework. You need an argument.

Package environment or options. Defaults, feature flags, a memoised registry, the current printing width. Ambient, documented, easy to override in a test by setting the option inside withr::with_options or by not reading the option when an argument was supplied.
Arguments. Anything that changes the correctness of a call. If a test must swap it, it is an argument, or it is a field of a handle that was built from an argument.
The hybrid that stays sane. client <- api_client_new(config = api_config_default()), and api_config_default() reads the option once. Callers who care pass a config they built themselves. Callers who do not care get the default. Nobody reaches through <<-.

This is also the answer to “a package environment versus a client that closes over the config.” The package environment is a process-lifetime default. The client is a value you chose to give identity because it acts. Functions that quietly call get_config() from the package environment are hard to test and hard to reason about, and they feel convenient for exactly as long as you have one config. The day you have two — prod and sandbox, this tenant and that tenant — the hidden lookup becomes the bug.

title: 11  Where State Lives
text:
11.4 Reactivity is the tell
The notebook’s guess about reference semantics was right, and it is the best reason to choose a handle on purpose. If a later step must observe that this object changed — invalidate a cache, advance a progress bar, refresh a token that other calls share — then identity is part of the feature. Values can imitate this with explicit returns and with reactive frameworks that diff old and new, and sometimes that imitation is the point. Shiny’s reactive graph is a disciplined version. It is a lot of machinery to reach for when an environment would have been the honest model.
The converse tell: if you never observe identity, a reference object is paying for a capability you do not use, and you are giving up the ability to treat the thing as a value in tests and in pipes. S7 getters and setters do not change this. A setter on a value returns a new value. A setter on a handle mutates. The syntax can be made to look similar. The addresses will not.

title: 11  Where State Lives
text:
11.5 Superassignment, one last time
<<- is the undeclared version of a handle. It can implement the same patterns, and people do, and the patterns work until the enclosure chain is not the one they imagined. Lexical scope is a feature when you are resolving a free variable on purpose. It is a liability when you are using it as a mutable store you refused to name.
If you want the pattern “scratch space inside a function, value out,” do that with a local environment and return a list or an S7 object. The environment dies with the call. The value carries the facts. That is the ST pattern from Chapter 5, performed by hand, and it is a good pattern. The moment the environment is returned, or stored in the package environment, you have built a handle. Then name it as a handle and give it a type, so the next reader does not have to discover the identity by calling lobstr::obj_addr.

title: 12  Types Without a Checker
text:
12.1 The ritual you have already been performing
The desire is not for a particular compiler. It is for the situation in which a name admits only the values that mean that name, in a shape you can rely on, with the structural work done by the runtime’s garbage collector instead of by a borrow checker. Rust, Zod, Pydantic, an S3 constructor ritual, and an S7 property are the same mental model at different distances from the bits. R’s gap is that defining the type is not a pleasant, first-class act. You assemble it.
That gap is not a reason to lower the standard. If the work is production work, invalid states are unrepresentable. “Mostly conventions” is how you describe a prototype, not a package other people call.
The S3 version of parse-don’t-validate is a small protocol, repeated until it becomes muscle:
That is “illegal states unrepresentable.” It is unrepresentable by convention, which means a later edit can build the object through new_* and skip validate_*, and the type system will not notice. The protocol works in the packages where someone is strict about the doors. It drifts in the packages where the doors multiply.
S7’s contribution is not a new philosophy. It is a place to put the protocol so the drift has to work harder:
Its cost is authoring. Next to a Zod schema or a Pydantic model, an S7 class is verbose, and the official examples often stop at class_any plus a check inside a method. That teaches the syntax. It does not teach the reason you reached for a class. The S7 design notes are the attempt to write the missing practice down: what knowledge the model carries, where a rule lives, when a property should itself be a class, how editable values differ from snapshots and from reference owners. This chapter will not repeat that book. It will connect it to the metal, and to the envy.

title: 12  Types Without a Checker
text:
new_* builds the structure and does not check
validate_* states the laws and fails with a classed error
the user-facing constructor calls both, and is the only door
as_* coerces at the boundary and then goes through the door
format_* / print / str make the value legible




property contracts live on the property
joint laws live on the class validator
the constructor is the door
generics are a stronger dispatch story when the verbs and the nouns both grow

title: 12  Types Without a Checker
text:
12.2 The envy is a diagnostic
Zod and Pydantic make parsing the default gesture. You write the shape once. Construction fails or you hold a value. Consumers trust the type. The authoring experience is the feature. People adopt the library because the schema is shorter than the bugs it prevents, not because they read an essay about bounds.
S7 can express the same designs. A property can name a class, a union, a base type, a validator, a getter, a setter. A class validator can state laws that mention more than one property. convert can sit at the edge where JSON becomes a domain value. The machinery is further along than the examples suggest. What is missing is the worn path: the way a competent author reaches for a reusable property the way a TypeScript author reaches for z.number().int().min(0).max(255). Until that path exists, production S7 will keep looking under-typed, not because the objects cannot carry the law, but because class_any is the path of least resistance and the checks leak back into the methods.
The metal already ratted this out. In the notebook, a property defined as p = class_any inspects as an S7_property record. The names visible in the dump include name, class, getter, setter, and validator. The record’s length is 6; the paste elides one name, so this book will not invent it. The getter, setter, and validator slots in that particular property are Nil. class points at the empty S7_any vector. The structure for a real property contract is allocated. The example left it blank and postponed the law to whoever uses p later.
That is the whole complaint, photographed. Filling those slots is the work. A scalar-or-null string is a type, expressed as a union or as a property validator, not as class_any followed by if (!is.null(x)) in every method. An enum of five statuses is a class or a property whose validator knows the five strings, not a character and a prayer. A color with channels in 0:255 stores the channels under validators and exposes brightness as a getter, so brightness cannot drift out of agreement with the channels. An API response becomes one class per reusable object, with coercion at the edge and nowhere else.







The law
Where it lives




This field’s shape, range, and presence
the property


These fields together
the class validator


Wire format into the domain
the constructor, or convert, at the boundary


What we do when we talk to the world
verbs on a handle, or generics on the values



Checks inside methods rediscover the law at every call site. They do not compose. A property validator composes: every constructor, every replacement, every subclass that reuses the property, gets the same door.

title: 12  Types Without a Checker
section: 12.3 S3 when you already own the ritual
text:
12.3 S3 when you already own the ritual
Use the manual protocol when the vocabulary is small, the type is a thin wrapper, and you already trust yourself to keep the doors closed. Use it when the community already speaks the class (data.frame, an httr2 response) and a formal property model would be a translation nobody asked for. Use S7 when you are inventing the model: schemas, configs, enums, validated quantities, anything that will grow a second property and a third invariant. Use neither as a costume. An S7 class full of class_any is a list with a longer error message. An S3 class with no constructor is a string someone set an attribute on.
The dispatch difference is real and secondary. S7’s generics are a better instrument when verbs and nouns multiply. They do not fix a model that was never written. Choose S7 when you want the contracts attached to the object and you are willing to fill in the slots the dump already showed you. Choose S3 when the ritual is short enough to see in one screen and you will actually perform it.

title: 12  Types Without a Checker
section: 12.4 Print methods are part of the type
text:
12.4 Print methods are part of the type
Hadley’s packages are the existence proof that this is not academic. A finished type has a format that tells the truth in one line, a print that uses it, and a str that does not dump the SEXP. That is not decoration on top of an object system. It is how a value announces itself in the REPL, which is still where R is used, including by the person who wrote the package and has forgotten the shape. Chapter 13 pushes this further, toward views as a separate contract. For this chapter it is enough to say that a constructor without a format method is half a type.
Functional composition is the other half of the same craft. Small verbs, each accepting a defended value and returning one, compose. A class hierarchy that you have to enter to get anything done does not compose with the pipe, the script, or the test. The OO in a good R package is the minimum that makes the verbs generic and the values meaningful. The rest is functions. That is a taste. It is also what the language is good at, once you stop apologizing for the missing checker and supply the parse yourself.

title: 12  Types Without a Checker
text:
12.5 Where to spend the verbosity
Verbose types and boring call sites means the bet paid off. Verbose call sites mean the rules were left in the methods. Move a constraint into a property until constructing the object feels as dull as calling integer(). Dull is the goal. The interesting thinking happens once, when you decide what the name admits, and then it stops happening in every function that receives one.
Do not spend the verbosity on temporary lists inside a function. A local list(a = 1, b = 2) does not need a class. Spend it at boundaries: the wire, the file, the public argument, the value you put in a package’s return position. Those are the places other code will otherwise rediscover the law, badly, under time pressure.
The companion book works the design consequences in detail: property versus class, presence versus default, snapshots versus reference owners, the checking ladder, dispatch as a vocabulary of verbs. Start at the overview if you want that argument at full length. The claim this chapter adds is only that the runtime is not the obstacle. The authoring path is. The nodes will happily carry a strict model. Someone has to write the model as if the slots were the point, because they are.

title: 13  Shown on Purpose
text:
13.1 The pipe carries objects
A type that cannot show itself is a schema with no error messages. The same instinct that wants a parser at the boundary wants a view at the boundary. Structure, validity, and presentation are one design surface, split into layers so they can change at different speeds.
R gets you part of the way by cultural habit. print, format, and str are generics, so a class can own its appearance without owning the console. cli raised the ceiling: a package can look like a small text interface, with semantic roles for alerts, progress, and inline values, instead of a pile of pasted strings. You can tell a finished package by the console. The unfinished ones dump print.default and apologize with a vignette.
PowerShell gets you the rest of the idea, and then shows you how an idea can outlive its file format.
Jeffrey Snover wrote the Monad manifesto on 8 August 2002. The public copy lives on Microsoft Learn and as a PDF. The sentence that matters, against a tradition of “prayer-based parsing” of text:
Downstream commands reflect on those objects. Format-Table is a command at the end of the pipeline, not a conversion that happens in the middle. The manifesto is explicit that once you have rendered text, you are back in the world of prayer. Formatting is a host concern. The objects survive until the host.
That is the alignment with the R taste, and it is worth saying without irony. The substrate is a large, formally specified object runtime. The experience on top is a shell: verbs, pipelines, streams, discoverable help. The object model is the backbone. It is not the user interface. R’s version is less formal and strangely similar. SEXPs are the backbone. Functions are the user interface. print is what the host does when the pipeline ends and a human is watching.

title: 13  Shown on Purpose
text: Instead of piping unstructured text, we pipe .NET objects.

title: 13  Shown on Purpose
section: 13.2 Format data is a view contract
text:
13.2 Format data is a view contract
Format.ps1xml files, and the views that replaced them, declare how a type is shown: a table, a list, a wide view, a custom view. The official description is about_Format.ps1xml. The important sentence in that document: the formatting affects the display only. It does not change which properties flow down the pipeline.
Beginning in PowerShell 6, the built-in views moved into the source code. The XML files from Windows PowerShell 5.1 are not how the default views are defined anymore. Custom Format.ps1xml files still work, and Update-FormatData still loads them. The file format is the part that aged. The separation did not. Wanting the idea “revamped into something better” is in agreement with the direction the shell already took. Keep the contract — a declarative view, distinct from the value, swappable by the host — and retire the ceremony that got you there in 2006.
The Extended Type System is the companion move. ETS can adapt how a type presents members and type names without you owning the class, which is how a shell stays useful in a world of ADO tables, WMI objects, and XML whose reflected shapes are not the shapes a human wants. The manifesto calls the piece an extended type reflector. You do not subclass FileInfo to make Get-ChildItem show Length and LastWriteTime. You project it.
S3 generics are a cousin of that reflector. format.my_class adds a view from outside the value. What R never grew is the declarative pack: a data file, reviewed like data, that says “this class renders like so in a console, and like so in a markdown table,” without the rendering buried in a method that mixes policy with string concatenation. cli themes and format methods are the craft version. They work. They are code, so they are harder to swap per host than a view definition would be. If you ever build the missing piece, build it as data. The method can interpret the data. The data should be the design.

title: 13  Shown on Purpose
text:
13.3 A short, unromantic history
The affection for this design sometimes gets told as a single arrow from Cairo to Longhorn to WinFS to .NET to PowerShell. The arrow is a mood, not a genealogy, and the mood survives a more accurate story.
COM gave Windows a binary notion of interface identity. IUnknown, vtables, reference counts, a contract you could implement from more than one language. It also gave the industry DLL hell. The idea that survived is metadata and interfaces, not the binary layout.
Cairo was an early-1990s attempt at an object-oriented operating system. It did not ship as conceived. Pieces of the thinking scattered into later Windows. It is not the parent of the CLR.
Longhorn’s WinFS was an attempt to make the filesystem a store of typed items. It was cut. It did not grow up into .NET. The dream — systems that speak in typed items rather than opaque files — is a recurring Microsoft dream, and it has failed as a product more than once. The failure does not make the dream stupid. It makes it a bad causal claim.
.NET is a managed runtime with serious metadata, designed around the turn of the century, informed by COM’s successes and scars and by other language runtimes. PowerShell is Monad: Snover’s bet that an administrative shell on that runtime should pipe objects and format at the edge. That bet shipped. It is the piece you can actually learn from, because it has docs, an object pipeline, streams, and a view layer you can point at.
Take the aesthetic and leave the arrow. Typed meaning in the middle. Declarative projection at the host. Mutation and I/O quarantined. The backbone can be SEXPs and generics, or CLR metadata and ETS. The shape of the program is the part worth copying.
DSC, mentioned in the same breath, is the instinct aimed at desired state instead of desired display: say what should be true, let the system converge. It is a different feature and the same love of declarative descriptions. This book does not have a chapter on configuration management. It has a chapter on the love.

title: 13  Shown on Purpose
section: 13.4 What to do in an R package this week
text:
13.4 What to do in an R package this week
You do not have format data. You have generics and cli. Use them as if the view were a contract.

Write format.<class> to return a character vector of the meaning, not a dump of the slots. One line if the value is a fact. A short block if the value is a document.
Write print.<class> as a thin caller of format, returning the value invisibly, so the REPL stays a conversation.
Use cli for situations: alerts, progress, inline code and values. Give the output semantic roles so a theme can restyle it.
Keep the view free of decisions. Formatting does not fetch, validate, or mutate. If print has a side effect beyond writing, the contract is already confused.
When a value has more than one useful projection — a one-line summary, a verbose dump, a markdown row — make those named functions, not flags buried in print. PowerShell’s table-versus-list split is the model. You can ship it as format and format_details long before you have a view file format.

And connect it back to streams. The view is what success looks like. The condition system is what the other channels look like. A package that formats its values and signals its situations, and never cat()s either, feels finished because both contracts are present. A package that only computes the right answer still feels like a sketch. The console is part of the product, especially in a language whose main instrument is a conversation.

title: 14  Data Drives the Design
text:
14.1 What to stop arguing about
The machinery is secondary. OO or functional, compiled or collected, checked by rustc or by a constructor: those are how you pay for a smaller set of demands.
Names. A curated vocabulary. Domain-driven design’s ubiquitous language, scaled to a package or to one developer’s system, not reserved for a program with the word “enterprise” in the brief. The names are the model. If you cannot say the sentence without inventing a noun, the model is missing a noun. If you have three nouns for one fact, the model is avoiding a decision.
Types. A name admits only valid, structured values. The structure is known. The meaning is the name, not the payload. An integer64 that is secretly a double is a tolerated lie at the physics layer; at the vocabulary layer the name still has to mean a 64-bit integer, and the verbs have to keep the lie from leaking. A status that is secretly any string is a lie at the vocabulary layer, which is worse, because nothing downstream can recover the five legal values by inspecting the SEXPTYPE.
Views. How a value appears is configurable in the best systems and hand-written in R, and in both cases it is part of the contract. The view is not the value. Format at the host.
Verbs. Functions do the work. Open dispatch attaches them to types without trapping them inside types. A workflow is a composition of verbs that values flow through. When a step needs identity — a socket, a token, a conversation — the value flowing through is a handle, and the handle is explicit.
Data first. The shapes in the domain drive the types. You do not start from a class hierarchy you admired in another codebase and pour the data in. You start from the record, the enum, the document, the event, and you ask what must be true of each. The functions arrive when the shapes can survive a round trip through a verb without losing a law.
Everything earlier in the book is a detail under this picture.
The header, the three empties, cons against vectors, reference counts, ALTREP, and promises explain why the values in the middle can be cheap and still behave like values. The context chapter explains why a handle is a different node, not a different mood. Signals explain how failures and narration stay structured while the values move. The lineage explains why the picture feels natural in R and slightly uphill to enforce. The container rules are the picture applied to one API. The type chapter is the picture applied to a language that will not write the boxes for you. The appearance chapter is the view box, which people skip and users feel.
Whether a given package is “really OO” is not a useful argument. Whether its names are curated, whether its constructors parse, whether its printers tell the truth, and whether its verbs are open where a stranger should be able to extend them: those are useful arguments. You can win them in S3, in S7, in Rust, in PowerShell, in a disciplined corner of Python. You can lose them in all five, loudly, with a lot of classes.
Composition over inheritance falls out of the same picture. Inheritance bundles “what I am” with “what I can do” and with “how I am stored.” The picture wants those separable. A subtype is a real tool when the domain has a real inclusion and the laws of the parent are laws of the child. It is a bad tool when what you wanted was a new verb, or a new view, or a nullable field. R’s generic functions make the good case easy and the bad case unnecessary. You can still build the bad case. The language is not going to slap the metaphor out of your hand.

title: 14  Data Drives the Design
section: 14.2 The stance, small enough to reuse
text:
14.2 The stance, small enough to reuse
Treat R as a Scheme-powered array language for having a conversation with data. Let the conversation discover the nouns. Then make the nouns boring: parsed, printable, and passed to verbs. Keep mutation in handles at the edge. Keep foreign runtimes behind interfaces that exchange objects and lifetimes, not surprise text. Pick one story for failure at each boundary.
The value illusion is what makes the middle of that program pleasant. You get to think in values while the runtime shares, delays, and sometimes never allocates. The illusion is not permission to forget the edge. At the edge, identity is real, the network is real, missingness is real, and the user’s eye is real. Name those too.
You were not messing around without a goal. You were checking, from the node header upward, whether a taste you already had was compatible with the machine you actually run. It is. The machine will not write the program in that taste. It will only stop punishing you for it, provided you stop asking a value to be a handle, a signal to be a string, and a name to be a hope.

title: Appendix A — Lab Notebook
text:
A.1 Where inspect comes from
This is the original session, retold as a sequence of probes. The point of the retelling is the order. A hypothesis was written down. The next call confirmed it, qualified it, or killed it. That rhythm is worth more than any particular flag.
The script is a private scratch file. What follows is the part that generalizes. Where a printed REF count depended on RStudio holding extra references, the count is reported as a phenomenon, not as a constant.
The file opens on the right question: is inspect itself a SEXP you can study, or a door into the C runtime? It is a door. .Internal(inspect(x)) calls do_inspect. The value you pass is the SEXP. The printer is an entry in the internals table. Chapter 2 decodes a line. The rest of this notebook assumes that decoding.
A classed list (structure(list(x = 1L), class = "obj")) showed the whole vocabulary at once: a VECSXP with OBJ and ATT, a child INTSXP, and an attribute LISTSXP whose tags were the symbols names and class. Those symbols were locked, saturated, and old (g1). The character data was a cached CHARSXP. One object, three worlds: generic vector, atomic vector, cons chain.

title: Appendix A — Lab Notebook
section: A.2 Nil, and the hypothesis that overreached
text:
A.2 Nil, and the hypothesis that overreached
NULL, c(), and pairlist() shared an address, type 0, REF(65535). identical() stayed true under the strict switches, including extptr.as.ref = TRUE. That flag does not speak to this comparison: NULL and c() are not external pointers. The comment drew the natural conclusion anyway: any genuinely empty thing is that cell.
list() and alist() retired the conclusion for generic vectors. Each was a fresh length-zero VECSXP. integer(), double(), character(), logical(), complex(), and raw() retired it for the atomics. The comment had guessed that lists were VECSXP because they need method dispatch. The type is older than that need. Dispatch consults the class and the OBJ bit. An empty list with no class is already not Nil. Chapter 3 is the write-up. The primitive-generic vectors printed next to the hypothesis (.S3PrimitiveGenerics, .internalGenerics) are about which verbs are wired into C, not about why the empty list exists.
typeof(character()) is "character" and the SEXP type is STRSXP. The comment’s STRSEXP was a reasonable coinage. The cache of individual strings is the CHARSXP layer underneath.

title: Appendix A — Lab Notebook
text:
A.3 Primitives
sum and + and c printed as builtins, type 8, saturated, old. [ printed as a special, type 7. Printing a primitive shows .Primitive("sum") rather than a body. That is the applicative-versus-raw split from Chapter 6, met in the wild. These types are not mythical. They are what typeof of the function returns, any time you ask.

title: Appendix A — Lab Notebook
section: A.4 A double wearing a class
text:
A.4 A double wearing a class
bit64::integer64() has typeof "double" and inspects as a REALSXP with OBJ, ATT, and class "integer64". The comment called this interesting and then, later, connected it to factors. Factors felt like they might be “more of an object” in the OBJSXP sense. They are not. is.object(factor(1)) is true because the OBJ bit is set. typeof is "integer". The historical SEXP types for factors were 11 and 12, and they were withdrawn. The “lie about storage” pattern is the living design. Chapter 6 keeps the two meanings of “object” apart so they can stay apart.

title: Appendix A — Lab Notebook
section: A.5 Conditions, left open on purpose
text:
A.5 Conditions, left open on purpose
The long comment is the seed of Chapter 7. Conditions look like a CLOS-style system, the surrounding culture uses them as exceptions, and errors-as-values (purrr, rlang results, validators) sit nearby unused. The comment’s own correction is the one to keep: it is S3 on a signaling foundation, not CLOS. The resemblance to Pitman is in the shape — signal, handle on the live stack, restart — not in the implementation. The frustration with catching an error only to throw another one is a layering point, not a reason to abandon signals.

title: Appendix A — Lab Notebook
text:
A.6 S7 classes are closures
S7::class_any inspected as a length-zero VECSXP with class S7_any. Not a class constructor. S7::new_class("myclass") inspected as a CLOSXP with attributes for the class metadata, a body that calls S7::new_object, and a parent whose body was already a BCODESXP inside the S7 namespace. typeof of the class object is "closure".
That dump is also where byte code, language objects, and the Nil formal list show up without anyone asking for them. A compiled package function contains a BCODESXP. A call in the body is a LANGSXP. An empty formal list is Nil. “Types you never see” are types you see the moment the value you asked about is implemented with them.

title: Appendix A — Lab Notebook
text:
A.7 R6 generators are environments
typeof(R6::R6Class()) is "environment". The inspect paste is long because the generator is an environment full of closures, and the clone method’s body is a program that allocates more environments, remaps function enclosures, locks them, and registers a finalizer for $finalize. The symbol <<- appears inside that generated code. So does .__enclos_env__. The class attribute on the generator is R6ClassGenerator.
This is the Scheme object, written out by a code generator. It is also a practical demonstration that <<- is not foreign to serious R. R6 uses superassignment inside a known enclosure, the object environment it just built. That is the declared version. The fragile version is the one where the enclosure is whatever happened to call you. Seeing both in the same afternoon is how the distinction becomes obvious.

title: Appendix A — Lab Notebook
text:
A.8 Weak references
rlang::new_weakref(new.env(parent = emptyenv()), value = "x") has typeof "weakref" and inspects as type 23, WEAKREFSXP. The comment asked whether this is only an rlang convention. The type is a runtime type. The comfortable constructor is a package. reg.finalizer is what base gives you for the adjacent problem. Chapter 6 puts external pointers next to weak references so the two stop sharing a single vague reputation.
The same stretch of the file quotes the internals manual on a fossil: “user databases,” apparently the old Omegahat RObjectTables package, an undocumented lookup hook. It is a good reminder that the manual still contains archaeology. Read it next to the source when a sentence seems to describe a feature you have never seen. Sometimes the feature is real and hidden. Sometimes it is a scar.

title: Appendix A — Lab Notebook
section: A.9 The question the dumps were heading toward
text:
A.9 The question the dumps were heading toward
The file then states the design question cleanly. Reference semantics make in-place change observable, which is what you want for invalidation, caches, and anything reactive. Values plus replacement functions can imitate some of that, at the cost of a new object. Low-level facts do not design a package by themselves. They tell you which promises the package is allowed to make. The rest of the file is an S7 experiment that takes the promise seriously.

title: Appendix A — Lab Notebook
section: A.10 An S7 assignment changes the address
text:
A.10 An S7 assignment changes the address
s_x was defined with a single class_any property. The class object was a CLOSXP. An instance was created. lobstr::obj_addr was recorded. my_x@p <- "aaa" was evaluated. The address changed. The new node was an OBJSXP with OBJ and ATT, class c("s_x", "S7_object"), a pointer back at the class, and a property record whose visible names included name, class, getter, setter, and validator.
That is the value illusion, holding, for a class system that people sometimes describe as “more OO” and therefore somehow reference-like. The replacement syntax looks like mutation. The address says a new value was born. R6 would have kept the address. The two dumps together are the fork in Chapter 5 and Chapter 11, obtained before any of those chapters were written.
The property record is the other souvenir. The slots for a strict property were present and, in this definition, empty. Chapter 12 hangs the authoring argument on that observation. The docs can show class_any. The node still has a place to put a validator. The next person who defines p gets to decide whether the place stays empty.

title: Appendix A — Lab Notebook
text:
A.11 What to rerun
When a R release moves, the probes worth repeating are the ones the verification script already pins, plus three that need a human eye:

inspect(1:1e9) and see whether you are looking at an ALTREP node rather than a billion integers
lobstr::ref before and after x[1] <- on a shared vector, and watch the count force a copy
a withCallingHandlers / withRestarts pair small enough to feel the stack stay alive, next to a tryCatch that unwinds it

The script in verification/ guards the claims that should not drift: Nil’s identity with c() and pairlist(), the independence of list(), the types of the typed empties, the factor representation, and builtin versus special. If one of those fails, the book is describing a different R than the one you have, and the book loses.

title: Appendix B — Open Questions
text:
B.1 The symbol gp bits
A reading gets to live in a chapter when a manual, the source, or a probe supports it. These are the ones that do not clear that bar yet. They are recorded so the chapters do not quietly upgrade them into mechanisms.
Inspect lines for symbols in the original session carried gp values such as 0x4000, 0x5000, 0x6000, 0x7000, and 0x8000, often next to LCK and “(has value)”. CHARSXP lines carried smaller values such as 0x60 and 0x61, and inspect already translated the part a human needs (ASCII, cached). The general-purpose field is sixteen bits whose meaning depends on the type. The CHARSXP encoding section covers one dialect. The symbol dialect lives in the source, and this book does not publish a decoded table it has not checked bit by bit against that source.
What would close it: a short comment in src/main/inspect.c or the symbol macros in the headers, quoted next to one fresh dump, for the current R.

title: Appendix B — Open Questions
section: B.2 The sixth name on an S7_property
text:
B.2 The sixth name on an S7_property
A property built as class_any inspected as a length-6 record. The paste showed name, class, getter, setter, and validator, and elided the last name. Chapter 12 refuses to guess it. The argument does not depend on the sixth name. The five that are visible already include the slots a strict property would fill.
What would close it: S7:::prop_names() or the constructor in the S7 sources for the installed version, plus one inspect that does not elide.

title: Appendix B — Open Questions
section: B.3 Does S7 pin the class at REFCNTMAX?
text:
B.3 Does S7 pin the class at REFCNTMAX?
Before the replacement, the class closure in the session had a finite REF. Inside the instance dump after @p <-, the class node appeared saturated. That can happen because many holders exist (the instance, the binding, the IDE, internal caches) or because something called MARK_NOT_MUTABLE. Saturation is a one-way door in the macros: once the count hits the ceiling, decrement will not bring it back. Treating “S7 classes are immortal” as a mechanism would be an overread of one dump.
What would close it: a quiet session, lobstr::ref on the class before and after instantiation, and a look at whether S7 sets the count on purpose.

title: Appendix B — Open Questions
section: B.4 Base-level constructors for weak references
text:
B.4 Base-level constructors for weak references
The session reached for rlang::new_weakref and got a real WEAKREFSXP. reg.finalizer is base. A user-facing weak-map constructor in base, of the same shape as rlang’s, was not part of the session and is not claimed here. The distinction between “the runtime has the type” and “the standard library hands it to you” is the point of that section. A future base function would narrow the gap without changing the type.

title: Appendix B — Open Questions
section: B.5 1:n and ALTREP, on this R
text:
B.5 1:n and ALTREP, on this R
The design of ALTREP is documented. The session that seeded this book did not paste inspect(1:1e9). Whether a given R build still represents that sequence compactly, and how inspect spells the ALTREP class name, is a probe worth running and not a fact this text pretends to have run.

title: Appendix B — Open Questions
text:
B.6 User databases
R Internals on environments still mentions “user databases” and points, a bit sheepishly, at the former Omegahat package RObjectTables. The manual calls the hook under-documented. Treat it as archaeology until you have a current C caller. It is not a third environment model you should design a package around.

title: Appendix B — Open Questions
section: B.7 Two PowerShell docs, one introduction date
text:
B.7 Two PowerShell docs, one introduction date
about_Output_Streams and about_Redirection agree on the stream numbers and disagree, in places, about which PowerShell version introduced warning, verbose, and debug as redirectable streams. This book uses the numbers and the roles, which agree, and does not adjudicate the version history.

title: Appendix B — Open Questions
section: B.8 What would change a recommendation
text:
B.8 What would change a recommendation
The container split (value for facts, handle for capabilities) would weaken if ordinary S7 replacement stopped changing object identity, or if environments grew copy-on-modify of their bindings. Neither is likely. The recommendation to fill S7 property slots instead of checking in methods would weaken if property validators stopped running on replacement. The S7 design notes keep a ledger of that kind of version-sensitive mechanic; defer to it for S7 behavior, and re-check after a major S7 release.
The recommendation to prefer calling handlers over tryCatch would not survive a problem whose correct policy is always “this attempt is over.” It is a default, not a law. The law is that the choice should be made on purpose, in one place, with a class a caller can see.

title: Appendix C — Glossary
text:
Terms for the distinctions this book keeps needing. Each one points at the chapter that gives it a home. Popups in the text use the same definitions.

ALTREP

A framework for giving an ordinary SEXPTYPE a different payload: a compact sequence, a deferred string, a mapped vector, a cached answer to “are you sorted?” See the value illusion.

Condition

A classed signal. Handlers can run while the stack is still live, or they can unwind. See signals.

Cons cell

A heap node with a head (CAR), a tail (CDR), and an optional name (TAG). Pairlists and calls are chains of them, ending at Nil. See cons and vectors.

Copy-on-modify

The rule that a shared ordinary vector is duplicated before a write, so other names keep the old value. See the value illusion.

Functional core

The part of a program that decides on values. The imperative shell around it is where effects, handles, and hosts live. See where state lives.

Generic vector

R’s user-facing list. One header plus a contiguous array of SEXP pointers. Type VECSXP. See three empties and cons and vectors.

Immortal

A node the collector must not free and the mutator must not modify. The reference count is pinned at REFCNTMAX, 65535. Nil is the canonical case. See the header.

Open verb

An operation that lives outside the type, so new nouns can join it and new verbs can be taught to old nouns. See open verbs.

Promise

A delayed argument: an expression, an environment, and eventually a value. Forced at most once. See the value illusion.

Reference owner

An object whose identity is part of the API. Aliases observe the same evolving state. See where state lives.

Restart

A named way to resume from a condition at the point where it was signaled, if someone established one. See signals.

Ubiquitous language

The curated names of a domain, shared by the code, the console, and the people working in it. See the law and data drives the design.

Value illusion

The public story that ordinary R objects behave as values, sustained by sharing, reference counts, delayed copies, and sometimes by never allocating the payload at all. See the value illusion.

View

How a value is shown. A separate contract from what the value is. See shown on purpose.

title: Appendix D — Sources
text:
D.1 The runtime, primary
The chapters link out at the point of use. This is the same shelf, grouped so you can see what kind of document each one is. Manuals beat blog posts. Source beats manuals when they disagree. Papers beat this book’s readings of the papers.

title: Appendix D — Sources
text:
R Internals, for R 4.6.1 (2026-06-24). SEXPTYPEs, the header, allocation classes, environments, attributes, special primitives, the character cache. The manual warns that it is a work in progress. Believe it, and check the source when a sentence is load-bearing.
The R Language Definition. The C-syntax / Lisp-and-APL-semantics paragraph, and the chapter on computing on the language.
src/main/memory.c in the wch/r-source mirror. Nil’s initialization, node classes, the generational heap. The comment “or armageddon happens” is not a joke you need to improve on.
src/include/Defn.h. REFCNTMAX, MARK_NOT_MUTABLE, the increment and decrement macros that refuse to move a saturated count.
Luke Tierney, Notes on Reference Counting in R. The design note from when reference counting was still opt-in. Read it for motivation and for the list of holders that deliberately do not count. Do not read it as a description of the compile flags in a current release. Current dumps print REF(n) because the switch happened.
Luke Tierney, Gabe Becker, and Tomas Kalibera, ALTREP: Alternative Representations for R Objects. The design note. The 2017 DSC slides circulate as a PDF; the tech-doc index is developer.r-project.org/TechDocs.

text:
D.2 The language, primary

John M. Chambers, S, R, and Data Science, The R Journal 12/1 (2020). The three principles, in his wording, with the 1976 blackboard and the reason there are no scalars. The book he points at is Extending R (Chapman and Hall/CRC, 2016), pages 4–11.

httr2, ellmer, cli, and rlang::try_fetch().
The companion design manual: S7 Design Notes.

title: Appendix D — Sources
text:
D.3 Conditions, types, and shells

Robert Gentleman and Luke Tierney, A Prototype of a Condition System for R. Exiting handlers versus calling handlers, from the people who put the mechanism in the language.
Kent M. Pitman, Condition Handling in the Lisp Language Family (2001). The Common Lisp mechanism itself is HyperSpec chapter 9.
Alexis King, Parse, don’t validate (2019).

Gary Bernhardt, Boundaries (SCNA 2012). The phrase “functional core, imperative shell” is his screencast of that name, dated 2012-07-12: Functional Core, Imperative Shell.
Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design (Addison-Wesley, 2003). Ubiquitous language: one shared vocabulary for the people and the model. Scaling that habit down to a package is this book’s recommendation, not a sentence from the book.
The Rust book, chapter on traits and the Rust API guidelines. Read these before repeating the “R is just like Rust” line to someone who writes Rust. The shared posture is open operations over types. The ownership story does not transfer.

section: D.4 PowerShell and the view layer
text:
D.4 PowerShell and the view layer

D.5 What not to cite this book for
Do not cite it for a guarantee about a future R, or for S7 behavior past what the S7 design notes have rechecked. Do not cite the Cairo / WinFS paragraph as a history of .NET; it is a warning against a bad history. Do not cite a REF count from an IDE session as a property of an expression. Cite the manuals, the source, and the probes in verification/ for anything that has to survive contact with a different machine.
